Codependency and boundaries

Am I Codependent? A Self-Test for Families of Alcoholics

Twenty statements, a simple scoring guide, and a sober alcoholic's inside view - without judgment or diagnosis.

Steven H. White · approximately 8 min read

“This isn't a character flaw, and it isn't weakness. It's adaptation.”

This self-test does not replace a professional assessment. It is designed to help you notice a pattern and find a starting point.

Maybe you've heard the word before: codependency. Maybe someone said it about you, or you read it somewhere, and the question stuck: am I like that? Or do I just love him and try to help?

This article will help you see your own situation more clearly. It isn't a judgment and it isn't a diagnosis. It's a mirror.

What is codependency?

Codependency isn't an official medical diagnosis. It's a description. It refers to the pattern where someone living with a dependent person gradually organizes their life around the other person's drinking: watching, controlling, covering up, and slowly losing their own needs, feelings and boundaries along the way.

Important: this isn't a character flaw, and it isn't weakness. It's adaptation. In an unpredictable situation, people do what works in the short term: pay closer attention, take on more, ask for less. The problem is that what helps you survive in the short term wears you down in the long term.

I saw from the inside how they adapted

During my drinking years I promised again and again, explained, and believed I had things under control. Meanwhile the people around me were watching, worrying, adapting, and trying to hold together what kept falling apart.

I didn't see it back then. Today I know that while I was drinking, they were doing a different job: keeping me going, on the outside and on the inside. That work came at a price, and I wasn't the one who paid it.

How everyone around me adapted

For me, lying started as a tiny drop. I needed money for an original cassette, bought a copied one, and the difference went on drink. I needed more for the class fund than was actually being asked for. That turned into twenty years, and if I wrote it all down, it would fill ten encyclopedias. In the end I was begging for money with shaking hands and selling everything I owned. What started as a drop became a tsunami, and nothing could stop it.

They say it all starts with one lie. What I really see looking back are the reactions. I learned how people reacted to me, and I learned how to use that.

When I was completely finished, in the deepest stage of my alcoholism, everyone was already handling everything for me. The worst part is that for a long time I didn't even grasp it. It's shameful, but that's how it was.

What it really cost them only hit me when, sober, I had to handle real life myself and there was nobody left to help. In my forties, I was inexperienced in my own life. That was the hardest lesson I ever paid for, and it still comes back to me.

They say karma pays you back. I buried my parents with dignity, my relationship with my wife is tolerable, and with my son it's almost perfect. But what my family did for me for years, I only understood when I had to do it myself.

The self-test

Read the statements and count how many you would answer with “yes, that's me.” Don't think too long about each one. Your first answer is usually the most honest.

Watching and control

1. I often keep track of how much he has drunk, or count the bottles.
2. I know in advance what the evening will be like, depending on whether he has been drinking.
3. I check his phone, his bag or his car for alcohol.
4. I have tried hiding or pouring away the alcohol.

Covering up

5. I have made excuses for him to family, friends or his workplace.
6. I have lied so that his drinking wouldn't come out.
7. I avoid inviting people over because I don't know what state he'll be in.
8. I'm ashamed of what happens at home, so I tell very few people anything.

Self-sacrifice

9. I have taken over tasks that should be his.
10. I can't remember the last time I did something just for myself.
11. I adjust my own plans to his condition.
12. I feel that if I don't hold everything together, it will all fall apart.

Feelings

13. My mood depends on what kind of day he's having.
14. I often feel guilty, even when I haven't done anything.
15. I have felt that I am to blame for his drinking.
16. I'm often angry, but I don't show it because it would only make things worse.

Boundaries

17. I have accepted explanations while knowing they weren't true.
18. I have said “if this happens one more time...” more than once, and then nothing happened.
19. I find it hard to say no, even when I really want to.
20. I feel I have no right to complain, because he has it harder.

Scoring

0-5 yes: You probably still have your own boundaries, but pay attention to the statements you said yes to. These are the earliest signs.

6-12 yes: Part of your life already revolves around his drinking. That isn't failure, it's a signal: time to look after yourself a little too.

13-20 yes: It looks like you're carrying a lot on your own, and your own life has been pushed into the background. You don't have to solve this alone. It's worth looking for support, from a counselor or in a family support group.

If you counted a lot of yeses

The first thing to know: these patterns made sense. They developed because they helped you survive a difficult situation. You don't have to be ashamed of them. But you don't have to live with them forever either.

And one more thing I know from my own story: everything you're doing for him now, he'll have to learn to do himself one day. The longer you carry it for him, the later he starts.

Change doesn't start with doing everything differently at once. It starts with noticing one single pattern, and responding differently once, just once.

A few first steps

Pick one statement from the list that hurts the most. Watch for a week when and how it shows up.

Do something for yourself that doesn't depend on him. A walk, a meetup, an hour you don't cancel.

Tell someone. A friend, a counselor, or people in a similar situation.

Find a family support group. Al-Anon and other self-help groups exist specifically for people who live with someone dependent.

Steven H. White - sober for ten years. Today he sees how much work his family did for him.

This is a mirror, not a diagnosis

Your answers do not label you. They can help you see where another person's drinking has begun to take over your own life.

One thing to remember

You don't have to solve this alone.

Change can begin with noticing one pattern and responding differently once.
